To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The age-adjusted mortality rate of breast cancer in Japanese women is significantly correlated with the intake of fat, animal-protein and dietary fiber.
the increased MCB in Japanese women is due to the long-term effects of a diet rich in fat and animal protein and low in dietary fiber.
the intake of a low fiber diet, high in fat and protein, is a risk factor for breast cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between breast cancer mortality and nutrient intake in Japanese women.
the relationship between the intake of dietary fiber and fat and mortality from breast cancer in Japanese females.
the relationship of dietary factors with MBC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a high fat, low-fiber diet is related to an increased risk of MBC.
a high fat, high animal protein, and low fiber diet may be associated with the increased MBC.

dietary fiber intake may play a protective role in breast cancer, but the effect of fat intake is more complex and may have an indirect influence through its effect on other factors, such as reproductive factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the high-fat, high-protein and low-fiber dietary pattern in Japan has a strong influence on the increased MBC.
the high-fat, high-protein, and low-fiber intake in Japanese women during the period from the 1950s to 1970s may have increased their MBC in the 1980s and 1990s.
the long-term effect of a high fat and animal protein diet and a low fiber diet on the risk of breast cancer is more important than the short-term effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not possible to predict the effect of a change in dietary intake on the risk of cancer by a short term study.
the time lag between the dietary intake of high fat, high animal protein and low fiber and the increased mortality from breast cancer in Japan was 20-32, 19-32, and 9-32 years, respectively.
the increased risk for breast cancer in Japanese women is associated with a long-term dietary pattern of high-fat, high-meat and low-fiber.
